notes: \clogic{The epigraph is the whole of the post's thesis. Nothing that follows adds an argument to it; the rest is a joke that restates it.}
\cpara{Recalls watching the Star Wars films as a young child and remembering Luke Skywalker as a cool Jedi.}
\cpara{Tells how rewatching years later showed Luke to be a whiny teenager.}

\cpara{``Yesterday'' refers to the author's post ``Trying to Try'' (1 October 2008), which opens with the same Yoda line and ends ``Don't try your best. Win, or fail. There is no best.'' That post carries the argument. It is not in the Highlights collection; this one is. A reader of the Highlights meets the joke without the argument it was written to illustrate.}
\cpara{Introduces an invented outtake in which Mark Hamill argues with George Lucas about the scene.}

\cpara{The quoted lines match the published script. What the post leaves out is what happens next. In the script, after Luke says ``You want the impossible,'' Yoda raises the X-wing and sets it on the shore. Luke says ``I don't... I don't believe it.'' Yoda answers: ``That is why you fail.'' The scene exists to show Luke's surrender as failure and to name its cause. The parody attacks the film for presenting as ordinary the very thing the film rebukes.}

\cpara{The complaint stated as characterization: a hero should show ``backbone.'' In the film this is the point of the scene. Luke is in training because he lacks what the ``Mark'' character demands; the story is about his getting it.}
\cpara{Has Lucas insist that Luke gives up, hears Yoda's lecture, and declares the task impossible.}
\cpara{The only line with an argument in it: a partial success is evidence that the task is possible. The post never states it in its own voice.}
\cpara{Has Hamill object that Luke would not abandon his own ship and strand himself, and propose showing him still trying a month later.}
\cpara{Has Hamill scale back: at least show Luke straining from sunset to sunrise before he calls it impossible.}

\cpara{The parody states the objection to itself and waves it away. A film cannot show five minutes of straining; stories compress. The author had written a year earlier, in ``The Logical Fallacy of Generalization from Fictional Evidence'' (October 2007), that storytellers' needs ``are not the same as the requirements of forecasting.'' Here a pacing decision is treated as evidence about people.}
\cpara{Has Hamill joke that if someone this feeble could master the Force, everyone would, since it would be easier than high school.}
\cpara{Has Lucas tell Hamill to leave the storytelling to him and just say his lines with conviction.}

\cpara{The post's thesis, and the only general claim in it: ``People wouldn't try for five minutes before giving up if the fate of humanity were at stake.'' It is a claim about human nature, supported by nothing but a film scene, spoken by a fictional version of a real man. That is generalization from fictional evidence, the fallacy the author wrote about in 2007. The stakes are also changed. The scene is about one man's spaceship. ``The fate of humanity'' is the author's concern, not the film's.}
